This isn't a workout sub but I'll give you a quick rundown which can hopefully get you started.

Two Workouts: A and B

Workout A:

-Squats (with barbell or dumbbells) or Leg Press (if you or your family has a history of back or knee problems)

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

-Chest Press (with barbell or dumbbells)

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

-Rows (any horizontal back row=> this can be an incline bench row, upright row, seated cable row, pick one)

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

Workout B:

-Deadlifts

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

-Pull ups (if you're too weak to do pull ups do chin ups, if you're too weak to do chin ups do assisted pull ups until you are strong enough)

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

-Shoulder Press (with dumbbells or barbell, upright or slight incline)

3 sets of 8-10

2 minutes of rest between sets

Workout Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. Alternate Workouts A and B each day you work out. For example, the first week you will do ABA, the next week you will do BAB, then ABA again.

When you can complete 3 sets of 10 reps for any exercise with good form increase the weight for the next session of that exercise by the smallest increment (usually 5 pounds).

Calculate your TDEE and eat 100-200 surplus calories above that. Eat at least 0.9 grams of protein per pound of body weight every day. Get approximately an even portion of your daily protein in 5-6 meals spaced out every 3-4 hours. So if you need 100 grams of protein per day eat 5 meals with ~20 grams of protein each every 3-4 hours (5 x 20 = 100).

Consult your doctor before starting a weight lifting program. Go to a reputable gym with professional trainers and have them teach you do every one of these exercises with perfect form. Don't waste money on supplements.

Good luck.

Note that what gyms advertise as "professional" is subjective. The weekend seminar some trainers get their certs from is a whole world apart from something like a nationally recognized cert like an NSCA, ACSM, or NASM cert. Then there's varying levels of certification, are they a personal trainer? Group fitness instructor? Cancer/post surgery fitness therapist? Or hell, even a tactical (think for the added gear of police, fire, and EMS) fitness instructor.

There is a MASSIVE disparity between the level of knowledge in today's community of fitness professionals, which is something the industry is slowly trying to address.
